Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims
When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

vignette: Sunita, a 37-year-old South Asian woman and shopowner in her community, has been living with the lasting effects of a sexual assault that occurred six months ago. Her trauma is deeply embedded in her daily life, manifesting through specific triggers and maladaptive strategies that have significantly altered how she interacts with the world. The assault took place late one evening as Sunita was closing her shop. A man who had been loitering outside approached her aggressively when he realized she was alone. The memory of this traumatic event is vivid but difficult to verbalize; Sunita can't seem to put the frightening moments into words. Instead, she relives them through flashbacks where it feels as if the experience were happening again. When people say things that remind her of her ex-partner, or when she hears names that are similar to those involved in the assault, these triggers plunge her back into a state of intense fear and guilt. Sunita's avoidance behaviors have become deeply ingrained over time. She avoids public transport entirely because it reminds her of the enclosed spaces where she felt trapped during the assault. These triggers not only reinforce her maladaptive strategies but also heighten her memories of the event, making them more vivid and terrifying each time they resurface. The guilt she feels when recalling the incident exacerbates her sense of vulnerability and danger. One particularly distressing memory involves a customer at her shop who resembles one of the individuals involved in the assault. Sunita's heart races as soon as she sees him, and the terror she experienced during the attack immediately returns. This non-verbal memory haunts her, often leading to flashbacks where she is re-experiencing the trauma while standing behind the counter at her shop. She feels unsafe unless her back is against a wall, where she can see everything happening in the room. Her fawn response - becoming overly compliant when feeling threatened - has also become a significant part of her coping mechanism. Sunita tries to appease others to avoid confrontation or re-traumatization, which further reinforces her sense of vulnerability and fear. This behavior extends beyond her personal life into her business, where she often defers to more assertive customers, even when it means missing out on potential sales. The cycle between triggers, memory, threat, and maladaptive strategies has become self-reinforcing. For instance, the guilt she feels each time a trigger resurfaces makes her retreat further into avoidance behaviors like staying away from public transport or becoming overly compliant in threatening situations. Her back-to-the-wall stance at home or in the shop is a clear manifestation of this cycle; every sudden movement by others immediately puts her on guard. Sunita's marriage has also been affected by these changes. Her husband notices that she has become more withdrawn and anxious, but he struggles to understand why she reacts so strongly to seemingly minor triggers. This isolation and avoidance have strained their relationship, making it difficult for Sunita to open up about her experiences even with someone who cares deeply for her. What finally brought Sunita to seek help was a particularly intense flashback at work that left her unable to function for several days. She is now most afraid of losing control in public and hopes that therapy can provide her with tools to manage these overwhelming feelings and return to a sense of safety and normalcy in her daily life. Sunita's journey toward healing will require addressing the intertwined cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat monitoring, and memory intrusions. She is determined to regain control over her experiences and interactions, hoping for a future where she no longer feels trapped by the shadows of her past.
